content.reading_text: Mamluk is an Arabic word meaning "one who is owned". A Mamluk was a soldier who had been bought as a child — and from 1250 to 1517 the sultanate of Egypt and Syria belonged to this corps and the households that came out of it. None of them chose it. They were children, and they were sold. The supply came mostly from the Kipchak grasslands north of the Black Sea, and from the late 1300s mostly from Circassia in the Caucasus. Boys of roughly ten to fifteen were bought from slave traders, shipped through Black Sea ports — often in Italian merchant vessels — and sold in Cairo. There they were converted to Islam and taught Arabic, then trained for around seven years in furusiyya: riding, archery from the saddle, the lance, the sword, and the care of horses. Sultan al-Salih Ayyub, the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt and a great-nephew of Saladin, housed his own corps on Rawda island in the Nile at Cairo. Bahr means the sea, and it also means the Nile — so they were known as the Bahriyya, the river regiment. They are the men who take over in Day 2. At the end of training a Mamluk was manumitted — legally freed — given a horse, weapons and a place in his master's household. He served as a free man for the whole of his career. His loyalty ran to the master who had bought him and to the cohort he had been trained with, a bond called khushdashiyya. The part that shaped everything else: his own sons could not inherit his place in the corps. They were free-born Muslims known as awlad al-nas, "the children of the people", and many became scholars, judges and officials — but the fighting corps itself was refilled every generation by buying new boys. That is the narrow, accurate version of the claim. It does not mean a Mamluk could leave his children nothing: property, money and position could be inherited. content_blocks.content:
Mamluk is an Arabic word. It means "one who is owned". A Mamluk was a soldier who had been bought as a child, and from twelve fifty to fifteen seventeen the sultanate of Egypt and Syria, ruled from Cairo, belonged to this corps and to the households that came out of it.

That is the careful way to say it, and it is worth saying carefully. Not every ruler of those years had that biography:, who takes the throne in Day two, did not, and neither did the free-born sons of Mamluks who sometimes reigned for decades. What was constant was the corps.

None of them chose it. They were children, and they were sold.

Rulers across the Islamic world had used purchased soldiers for centuries before this. What was unusual in Egypt was what happened next: the bought soldiers stopped serving the state and became it.

Where They Came From

In the first period, most came from the Kipchak grasslands north of the Black Sea — the open steppe that stretches from what is now Ukraine east toward the Caspian. From the late thirteen hundreds onward, most came instead from Circassia, in the Caucasus mountains.

Boys of roughly ten to fifteen were bought from slave traders. The supply came from warfare on the steppe, from famine, and from sale by families in hard years. They were moved through the Black Sea ports and shipped to Egypt, often in Italian merchant vessels, and sold in Cairo.

This was purchase, not conscription. It is worth keeping separate from the Ottoman devshirme, a levy of boys organised by a state, which is a different institution that developed under the Ottomans about a century and a half later.

The Training

In Egypt a new recruit was converted to Islam and taught Arabic. Then came the military education, called furusiyya, inside closed barracks: riding, archery from the saddle, the lance, the sword, wrestling, and the care and feeding of horses. It ran for something like seven years.

Sultan Ayyub, the Ayyubid ruler of Egypt, housed his own corps on Rawda island in the Nile at Cairo. Bahr means the sea, and it also means the Nile — so his men were known as the Bahriyya, the river regiment.

Freed at the End of It

At the end of training a Mamluk was manumitted — legally freed — and given a horse, arms, and a place in his master's household. This matters, and it is the part most often got wrong: the men who fought at Ain Jalut and the men who sat on the throne were legally free. The slavery is in how they were recruited, and in the fact that the system had to be renewed by buying more children.

His loyalty ran two ways: to the master who had bought and trained him, and to the cohort bought and trained alongside him, a bond called khushdashiyya. In the first generation he generally had no family of his own in Egypt, which is a large part of why the arrangement worked.

The Flaw Built Into It

A Mamluk's own sons could not inherit his place. They were free-born Muslims, known as awlad al-nas — "the children of the people" — and they could and did become scholars, judges, officials and merchants. What they could not do was take their father's position in the fighting corps.

So the corps was refilled every generation by buying new boys. A man could command an army and still not pass his place in it to his son.

One caution about what that does and does not explain. It does not mean a Mamluk could leave his children nothing — property, money, houses and position could all be inherited, and the sons of Mamluks did well in civil life. And it did not stop family power altogether:, the sultan of Day four, founded a line that held the throne on and off for nearly a hundred years. What was genuinely not heritable was membership of the fighting corps itself. Keep the claim that size, and it holds.
